boardAlignment.summary: Multi-store memory model, including the main stores and how their coding, capacity and duration differ.

definitionsAndCoreConcepts: The multi-store model distinguishes sensory memory, short-term memory and long-term memory as functionally different stages or stores in memory processing.
Sensory memory briefly retains incoming sensory information; attended information can enter short-term memory, and information that is encoded and retained can contribute to long-term memory.

Short-term memory has limited capacity and relatively brief duration without active maintenance, whereas long-term memory can retain information over much longer periods and has a much larger practical capacity.

Coding refers to the form in which information is represented. Different memory systems can show different coding tendencies, so coding, capacity and duration are distinct properties rather than interchangeable labels.
modelsResearchAndRelationships: The Atkinson-Shiffrin framework is useful for separating broad memory functions and information flow between sensory, short-term and long-term memory.
Later memory research, including working-memory accounts, shows that short-term processing is more differentiated than a single undivided temporary store.
evaluationAndLimits: The multi-store model is a simplified functional model rather than a literal map of three physical boxes in the brain.
The distinction between memory systems remains useful, but later evidence supports multiple forms of long-term memory and multiple components within working memory.
misconceptionsAndBoundaries: Information does not automatically pass through every store into long-term memory; attention, encoding and retrieval conditions matter.
Long-term memory should not be described as perfectly permanent or error-free simply because its duration and capacity are much greater than short-term memory.

revisionSynthesis: The board-specific requirement to compare coding, capacity and duration is alignment; the explanatory structure is independently authored from the open memory source.

boardAlignment.summary: Working-memory model, including the central executive, phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad and episodic buffer.

definitionsAndCoreConcepts: Working memory is a limited-capacity system for temporarily holding and manipulating information needed for ongoing tasks.
The central executive coordinates attention and allocates processing between working-memory components rather than acting as a large storage system.
The phonological loop supports temporary processing of speech-based and auditory-verbal information.
The visuospatial sketchpad supports temporary processing of visual and spatial information.
The episodic buffer provides a limited-capacity interface that can integrate information from different working-memory components and long-term memory into coherent episodes.
modelsResearchAndRelationships: Baddeley and Hitch's working-memory model replaced the idea of one undifferentiated short-term store with interacting components that can support partly separate tasks.
Dual-task findings and selective impairments are consistent with the idea that verbal and visuospatial processing can draw on partly distinct working-memory resources.
evaluationAndLimits: The component model explains why some simultaneous tasks interfere strongly while others interfere less, but the central executive is a broad control concept whose exact mechanisms are more difficult to specify.
Working-memory capacity is limited, but it should not be reduced to one fixed number that applies identically to every component, task and individual.
misconceptionsAndBoundaries: The phonological loop is not simply 'short-term memory'; it is one specialised component within a wider working-memory system.
The episodic buffer is not a permanent store; it temporarily binds information and links working memory with long-term memory.

revisionSynthesis: Revision keeps the exact component list as course alignment while using open psychology sources for the independently phrased functional explanation.

boardAlignment.summary: Forgetting through interference and retrieval failure when appropriate cues are absent or ineffective.

definitionsAndCoreConcepts: Proactive interference occurs when older learning disrupts the retrieval or learning of newer information.
Retroactive interference occurs when newer learning disrupts retrieval of older information.
Retrieval failure occurs when stored information is not successfully accessed because available retrieval cues do not sufficiently match or distinguish the target memory.
Encoding specificity describes the principle that retrieval is more effective when cues or contextual features available at recall overlap meaningfully with those present when the memory was encoded.
modelsResearchAndRelationships: Interference is most likely when competing memories are similar enough to create confusion or competition.
Context and other retrieval cues can improve access to a memory when they recreate diagnostically useful features of the original encoding conditions.
Cue effectiveness depends on cue-target overlap and distinctiveness; merely presenting any cue does not guarantee successful recall.
evaluationAndLimits: A retrieval failure should not automatically be interpreted as evidence that the memory trace has been erased; information can remain stored yet temporarily inaccessible.
Context-dependent recall is a conditional effect rather than a universal rule. Encoding-retrieval match can help, but matching nominal context does not guarantee functional retrieval.
misconceptionsAndBoundaries: Proactive and retroactive interference differ in the direction of disruption: old-on-new versus new-on-old.
Cue-dependent forgetting does not mean that every forgotten item will return if the original physical setting is recreated.

supports: better recall under congruent encoding and retrieval conditions

revisionSynthesis: Revision combines independently supported interference and cue-retrieval mechanisms under the exact-course forgetting requirement; no claim that all forgetting shares one mechanism is implied.

boardAlignment.summary: Eyewitness testimony: effects of questioning, post-event discussion and anxiety, plus cognitive-interview techniques.

definitionsAndCoreConcepts: Eyewitness memory is reconstructive and can be influenced by information encountered after an event.
Leading questions can alter a witness's report by suggesting details, assumptions or interpretations that were not independently retrieved from the original event.
Post-event discussion can produce memory conformity when co-witness information is incorporated into, or influences, an individual's later account.
Stress and anxiety can alter attention and memory formation, but their effects on eyewitness accuracy vary with intensity, timing, task demands and the type of information being remembered.
The cognitive interview is a structured interviewing approach designed to support fuller, accurate recall while minimising unnecessary interviewer contamination.
modelsResearchAndRelationships: Co-witness research demonstrates that discussion can transmit errors between witnesses, although collaboration can also sometimes support error correction; the key point is that another person's account can influence later memory reports.
The four classic cognitive-interview mnemonics are mental reinstatement of context, report everything, recall in a different order and recall from a different perspective.
Context reinstatement is grounded in encoding-retrieval specificity, and 'report everything' encourages witnesses to provide details they might otherwise omit.
Repeated cognitive interviewing can elicit additional correct information with relatively little loss of overall accuracy under controlled conditions.
evaluationAndLimits: The relation between anxiety or acute stress and eyewitness performance is not a simple rule that 'more anxiety always means worse memory'; stress can alter attention and downstream memory in different ways.
A cognitive interview can improve retrieval but does not guarantee accuracy, and interviewer behaviour, witness characteristics and the particular event can affect statement quality.
Post-event discussion effects should be distinguished from leading-question effects: both can introduce post-event information, but the social source and mechanism of influence differ.
misconceptionsAndBoundaries: Confidence in an eyewitness account is not, by itself, proof that every recalled detail is accurate.
The cognitive interview is not a technique for pressuring a witness to produce more details or to guess when unsure.
Post-event discussion does not inevitably create false memories; it creates an additional source of information that can influence later reporting.

supports: additional correct recall across repeated interviews

revisionSynthesis: Revision separates the exact AQA eyewitness categories from the underlying open evidence and explicitly avoids treating anxiety effects or cognitive-interview benefits as deterministic.

provenance.transformation: Reused already accepted Memory evidence, added rights-clear targeted sources only for the two documented depth bridges, and transformed the supported knowledge into Course Truth fields without using AQA prose as teaching corpus.
